extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political economy, economic historians, and policy thinkers
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Adam Smith’s principles explaining variation in commodity prices (wool, hides, meat, fish, precious metals) with examples from historical markets and policy effects. Useful for analyzing causes of price change and what price movements indicate about a country's wealth and improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement tends to raise real price of rude produce
rubrics_metrics.description: The real price of rude produce naturally tends to rise in the progress of improvement, though accidents can cause it sometimes to fall, remain the same, or rise more or less in the same period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a baseline expectation: as a country improves (population, cultivation, industry) demand and costs for many rude produces increase, but allow for variability from chance events or other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of some produce limited by related produce
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sorts of rude produce are appendages to others: e.g., the quantity of wool or raw hides any country can afford is necessarily limited by the number of cattle kept, which is determined by the state of improvement and agriculture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing supply potential, consider linked production constraints (stock levels) rather than treating commodities in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportability determines market extent and price response
rubrics_metrics.description: Commodities that are easily transported (wool without preparation, raw hides with little) have markets that often extend beyond the producing country, unlike perishable products like butcher’s meat which are confined to the domestic market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect transported goods to be more exposed to international competition and thus less likely to rise in price solely because of domestic improvement; policy effects (tariffs, export bans) altering transport or access will significantly change price dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of cultivation affects relative value of animal products
rubrics_metrics.description: In ill-cultivated, thinly inhabited countries the price of wool and hides bears a greater proportion to the value of the whole beast than in better-improved countries where demand for butcher’s meat is higher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relative prices (wool/hide vs whole beast) as indicators of agricultural development: high relative value of fleece implies large extent of land devoted to grazing and less cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement/population typically raises carcase price more than material parts
rubrics_metrics.description: As improvement and population progress, price of the whole beast (carcase) rises more than that of wool and hides because the market for meat expands with domestic population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting rising meat prices, attribute a larger share to domestic market expansion and rising domestic demand than to changes in internationally traded materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market proximity of manufacturing can increase material prices
rubrics_metrics.description: If manufactures that use wool or hides flourish domestically, the market for those materials is brought nearer and their price may increase by the amount previously spent on transportation to distant markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how development of downstream manufacturing changes local demand and raises raw material prices even if international demand is unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations can artificially confine markets and depress local prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Government restrictions (e.g., prohibitions on exporting wool, permissions to import duty-free) can confine a producer’s market to the home market and force competition with foreign materials, lowering domestic prices (example: English wool post-Edward III).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat legal/regulatory changes as causal variables: policy that restricts export or opens import will alter effective market size and prices regardless of natural improvement trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of carcass value adjusts when part-prices change
rubrics_metrics.description: If price falls for parts of an animal (wool, hide), the unpaid portion of value must be made up elsewhere (carcase) — how price divides across parts is indifferent to landlords/farmers provided total receipts are preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In welfare or distributional assessments, consider that shifts among component prices may leave producers' total receipts unchanged while altering consumer prices for specific goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of commodity price changes depends on land-use structure
rubrics_metrics.description: In unimproved countries where most land is for cattle, a fall in wool/hide prices will lower whole cattle price and thus rent and profit of such lands; in improved countries with diversified land use, the fall is absorbed by a relative rise in carcase price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the structure of land use (what proportion is grazing vs arable) to predict how component price changes affect land values, rents, and income distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fish supply limited by geography and becomes costlier for larger markets
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantity of fish is limited by proximity to sea/lakes/rivers and their fertility; scaling supply to meet much larger markets typically requires disproportionately more labor, vessels, and costly machinery, causing real price to rise with improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect fishing to show rising real prices as domestic demand expands, unless technology or access expands; analyze capital and distance costs when projecting supply growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of precious metals depends on purchasing power and mine fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of gold and silver in a country depends on (1) its power of purchasing (state of industry and annual produce) and (2) the fertility or barrenness of the mines which supply the commercial world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between demand-side (wealth/purchasing power) and supply-side (mine yields/discoveries) causes when explaining changes in bullion quantities and their price effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in bullion quantity affect nominal but not real wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: An increase or decrease in gold and silver alters nominal prices (money representation) but does not change the real annual produce of land and labour — real wealth remains the same even if the quantity of metals changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating low money prices with greater real wealth; analyze real quantities of goods and labour commanded rather than nominal money measures alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of precious metals is not a reliable indicator of national prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: High or low value of gold and silver proves only the barrenness or fertility of the mines supplying the world, not that a particular country was rich or poor at that time (examples: China richer but higher metal value; Spain/Portugal with mines yet poor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple indicators (production, cultivation, land improvement, income distribution) rather than precious-metal prices to infer a country's economic condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative prices between goods reveal social development
rubrics_metrics.description: Low money price of particular goods (cattle, poultry, game) in proportion to corn decisively demonstrates their abundance relative to corn, the low value of land occupied by them, and thus an unimproved or barbarous state of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross-commodity price ratios (especially against staple cereal prices) as diagnostic tools for the extent of land improvement and stage of societal development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform money-price rise would indicate metallic depreciation; uneven rises signal other causes
rubrics_metrics.description: If degradation of silver were the sole cause of rising money prices, it would affect all goods equally; observed unequal rises (some provisions rising more than corn) imply additional, commodity-specific causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing inflationary phenomena, test whether price rises are uniform; if not, investigate commodity-specific supply/demand changes, seasonal effects, or policy interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implications differ by cause of price rises (silver fall vs land improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If price rises are due to a fall in silver’s value, pecuniary rewards (wages) should be augmented proportionally to preserve real recompense. If rises result from increased land fertility and higher land-derived incomes, adjustments to wages are more complex and may not be warranted equally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For wage and public-pay policy, first diagnose whether price changes stem from monetary (bullion) causes or real resource/production changes; respond differently depending on cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural improvement alters relative food prices (animal up, vegetable down)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extension of improvement and cultivation raises prices of many sorts of animal food (by converting land to corn land) and lowers prices of many vegetable foods (by increasing abundance and introducing new staples like potatoes and maize).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating living standards and compensation, consider offsetting effects: rising animal food prices may be partially compensated by falling vegetable food prices and new, cheaper staples.
